claim: Bacteria surround themselves with peptidoglycan, an adaptable enclosure that contributes to cell shape and stability.
source: Bacteria surround themselves with peptidoglycan, an adaptable enclosure that contributes to cell shape and stability.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in microbiology supported by extensive literature and is presented as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Peptidoglycan assembly relies on penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) acting in concert with SEDS-family transglycosylases RodA and FtsW, which support cell elongation and division respectively.
source: Peptidoglycan assembly relies on penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) acting in concert with SEDS-family transglycosylases RodA and FtsW, which support cell elongation and division respectively.
evidence: This statement summarizes established knowledge about peptidoglycan synthesis mechanisms.

claim: In Bacillus subtilis, cells lacking all four PBPs with transglycosylase activity (aPBPs) are viable.
source: In Bacillus subtilis, cells lacking all four PBPs with transglycosylase activity (aPBPs) are viable.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (McPherson and Popham, 2003) as noted later in the manuscript.

claim: The alternative sigma factor σI is essential in the absence of aPBPs.
source: Here, we show that the alternative sigma factor σI is essential in the absence of aPBPs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and related experiments.

claim: Defects in aPBP-dependent wall synthesis are compensated by σI-dependent upregulation of an MreB homolog, MreBH.
source: Defects in aPBP-dependent wall synthesis are compensated by σI-dependent upregulation of an MreB homolog, MreBH, which localizes the LytE autolysin to the RodA-containing elongasome complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data (Figure 4E) and complementation experiments (Figure 5).

claim: MreBH localizes the LytE autolysin to the RodA-containing elongasome complex.
source: Defects in aPBP-dependent wall synthesis are compensated by σI-dependent upregulation of an MreB homolog, MreBH, which localizes the LytE autolysin to the RodA-containing elongasome complex.
evidence: This is supported by prior literature (Carballido-López et al., 2006) as cited in the manuscript and by the functional data presented.

claim: Cells unable to activate the σI stress response acquire gain-of-function mutations in the essential histidine kinase WalK.
source: Suppressor analysis reveals that cells unable to activate this σI stress response acquire gain-of-function mutations in the essential histidine kinase WalK, which also elevates expression of sigI, mreBH and lytE.
evidence: This is supported by whole-genome sequencing of suppressor mutants and subsequent characterization as described in the Results section.

claim: Gain-of-function mutations in WalK elevate expression of sigI, mreBH and lytE.
source: Suppressor analysis reveals that cells unable to activate this σI stress response acquire gain-of-function mutations in the essential histidine kinase WalK, which also elevates expression of sigI, mreBH and lytE.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression measurements shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The σI regulatory pathway balances directional peptidoglycan synthesis from the elongasome complex with the more diffusive action of aPBPs.
source: These results reveal compensatory mechanisms that balance the directional peptidoglycan synthesis arising from the elongasome complex with the more diffusive action of aPBPs.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the collective experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: PG functions as a large, covalently linked macromolecular enclosure and is actively remodeled to allow cell growth and division.
source: PG functions as a large, covalently linked macromolecular enclosure and is actively remodeled to allow cell growth and division.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field supported by the cited references (Egan et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2017).

claim: The basic processes of PG synthesis are broadly conserved.
source: The basic processes of PG synthesis are broadly conserved, and the detailed pathways are well documented.
evidence: This is established knowledge in microbiology.

claim: PG synthesis initiates with the diversion of sugars from central metabolism to form N-acetylglucosamine (NAG) and N-acetylmuramic acid (NAM).
source: PG synthesis initiates with the diversion of sugars from central metabolism to form the two amino-sugars, N-acetylglucosamine (NAG) and N-acetylmuramic acid (NAM), and the incorporation of amino acids to form the stem peptide (Barreteau et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the citation to Barreteau et al., 2008.

claim: The ultimate product of cytosolic PG synthesis reactions is lipid II.
source: The ultimate product of these cytosolic reactions is lipid II, a disaccharide pentapeptide precursor unit linked to an undecaprenyl pyrophosphate carrier lipid (van Heijenoort, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the citation to van Heijenoort, 2007.

claim: Lipid II is flipped across the membrane.
source: Lipid II is flipped across the membrane (Sham et al., 2014; Meeske et al., 2015) where it interacts with two key enzymatic activities to assemble the PG layer: a transglycosylase (TG) function joins the disaccharide unit to form long, linear chains of alternating NAG-NAM residues, and a transpeptidase (TP) activity crosslinks a subset of the pentapeptide side chains to link the glycan strands together.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sham et al., 2014 and Meeske et al., 2015.

claim: A transglycosylase function joins the disaccharide unit to form long, linear chains of alternating NAG-NAM residues.
source: Lipid II is flipped across the membrane (Sham et al., 2014; Meeske et al., 2015) where it interacts with two key enzymatic activities to assemble the PG layer: a transglycosylase (TG) function joins the disaccharide unit to form long, linear chains of alternating NAG-NAM residues, and a transpeptidase (TP) activity crosslinks a subset of the pentapeptide side chains to link the glycan strands together.
evidence: This is established knowledge about peptidoglycan synthesis.

claim: A transpeptidase activity crosslinks a subset of the pentapeptide side chains to link the glycan strands together.
source: Lipid II is flipped across the membrane (Sham et al., 2014; Meeske et al., 2015) where it interacts with two key enzymatic activities to assemble the PG layer: a transglycosylase (TG) function joins the disaccharide unit to form long, linear chains of alternating NAG-NAM residues, and a transpeptidase (TP) activity crosslinks a subset of the pentapeptide side chains to link the glycan strands together.
evidence: This is established knowledge about peptidoglycan synthesis.

claim: Insertion of new glycan strands requires endopeptidases that can cleave existing crosslinks to facilitate cell wall expansion.
source: Crucially, insertion of new glycan strands requires endopeptidases that can cleave existing crosslinks to facilitate cell wall expansion (Singh et al., 2012; Hashimoto et al., 2012; Do et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Singh et al., 2012; Hashimoto et al., 2012; Do et al., 2020.

claim: Beta-lactam antibiotics account for more than 60% of the global antibiotic market.
source: One class of PG-targeting antibiotics, the beta-lactams, account for more than 60% of the global market (Klein et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Klein et al., 2018.

claim: Beta-lactam antibiotics interfere with PG synthesis by covalently modifying penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs).
source: Beta-lactam antibiotics interfere with PG synthesis by covalently modifying penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), named for their affinity for the first widely used member of this drug family.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the citation to Tipper and Strominger, 1965.

claim: All PBPs have transpeptidase activity.
source: All PBPs have TP activity, and beta-lactams mimic the substrate of the transpeptidation reaction (Tipper and Strominger, 1965).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Tipper and Strominger, 1965.

claim: Beta-lactams mimic the substrate of the transpeptidation reaction.
source: All PBPs have TP activity, and beta-lactams mimic the substrate of the transpeptidation reaction (Tipper and Strominger, 1965).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tipper and Strominger, 1965.

claim: Class A PBPs (aPBPs) have both transglycosylase and transpeptidase activity.
source: Many PBPs also have TG activity, and these bifunctional PBPs are designated class A PBPs, or aPBPs (McPherson and Popham, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to McPherson and Popham, 2003.

claim: Class B PBPs (bPBPs) only have transpeptidase activity and must work in coordination with enzymes that provide transglycosylase activity.
source: Other PBPs, designated bPBPs, only have TP activity, and must work in coordination with enzymes that provide TG activity (Wei et al., 2003; Taguchi et al., 2019; Rohs et al., 2018; Özbaykal et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wei et al., 2003; Taguchi et al., 2019; Rohs et al., 2018; Özbaykal et al., 2020.

claim: PG synthesis can be regulated as a function of cell growth, division, nutritional status, and in response to externally imposed stresses such as the action of antibiotics.
source: Moreover, PG synthesis can be regulated as a function of cell growth, division, nutritional status, and in response to externally imposed stresses such as the action of antibiotics (Delhaye et al., 2019; Typas et al., 2012; Helmann, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Delhaye et al., 2019; Typas et al., 2012; Helmann, 2016.

claim: The sites of PG synthesis during cell elongation are correlated with cytoskeletal filaments assembled from MreB and its paralogs, MreBH and Mbl.
source: Seminal work in this system established, for example, that the sites of PG synthesis during cell elongation seem to be correlated with cytoskeletal filaments assembled from MreB and its paralogs, MreBH and Mbl (Kawai et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kawai et al., 2009.

claim: PG synthesis during elongation occurs in arcs that are perpendicular to the long axis of the cell.
source: This synthesis occurs in arcs that are perpendicular to the long access of the cell and is driven by a putative complex known as the elongasome (Garner et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Garner et al., 2011.

claim: Cell division occurs at mid-cell during vegetative growth and is directed by FtsZ in a complex called the divisome.
source: Cell division, in contrast, occurs at mid-cell during vegetative growth and is directed by a different cytoskeletal filament, FtsZ, in a complex called the divisome (Mahone and Goley, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mahone and Goley, 2020.

claim: A strain lacking all four known aPBPs was viable and still synthesized an apparently normal PG layer.
source: A key finding that challenged our understanding of PG synthesis in B. subtilis was the observation that a strain lacking all four known aPBPs was viable and still synthesized an apparently normal PG layer (McPherson and Popham, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McPherson and Popham, 2003.

claim: The missing transglycosylase activity in aPBP-deficient cells is insensitive to inhibition by moenomycin.
source: This implied that there must be another protein with TG activity and, unlike aPBP-associated TG activity, this activity was insensitive to inhibition by moenomycin (MOE).
evidence: This is an inference based on the viability of aPBP-deficient cells and the known specificity of moenomycin.

claim: Moenomycin activates the σM stress response.
source: MOE, like many PG synthesis inhibitors, activates the σM stress response (Mascher et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mascher et al., 2007.

claim: sigM null mutants are highly moenomycin sensitive.
source: Moreover, sigM null mutants are highly MOE sensitive (Mascher et al., 2007), which suggested that the missing TG might be part of the σM regulon.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mascher et al., 2007.

claim: The elongasome-associated transglycosylase has been identified as the SEDS family protein RodA.
source: Indeed, the elongasome-associated TG has been identified as the SEDS family protein RodA (Meeske et al., 2016; Emami et al., 2017), a known member of the σM regulon (Eiamphungporn and Helmann, 2008; Helmann, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Meeske et al., 2016; Emami et al., 2017.

claim: RodA is a known member of the σM regulon.
source: Indeed, the elongasome-associated TG has been identified as the SEDS family protein RodA (Meeske et al., 2016; Emami et al., 2017), a known member of the σM regulon (Eiamphungporn and Helmann, 2008; Helmann, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Eiamphungporn and Helmann, 2008; Helmann, 2016.

claim: FtsW provides transglycosylase activity in the context of the divisome.
source: A RodA paralog, FtsW, provides TG activity in the context of the divisome (Taguchi et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Taguchi et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2018.

claim: During cell elongation in B. subtilis, the bulk of PG synthesis is provided by the elongasome, with RodA serving as transglycosylase and PBP2a and PbpH serving as transpeptidase.
source: Our current understanding of PG synthesis during cell elongation in B. subtilis suggests that the bulk of synthesis is provided by the elongasome, with RodA serving as TG and PBP2a and PbpH, and perhaps also aPBPs, serving as TP (Emami et al., 2017; Meeske et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Emami et al., 2017; Meeske et al., 2016.

claim: The action of the elongasome is directional, largely oriented perpendicular to the long cell axis, and is balanced by a more diffusive activity of aPBPs.
source: This action is directional, largely oriented perpendicular to the long cell axis, and is balanced by a more diffusive activity of aPBPs (Dion et al., 2019; Vigouroux et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dion et al., 2019; Vigouroux et al., 2020.

claim: Cells that rely exclusively on the elongasome for growth are longer and thinner.
source: Cells that rely exclusively on the elongasome for growth are longer and thinner, whereas those that rely predominantly on aPBPs tend to be wider and shorter (Dion et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dion et al., 2019.

claim: Cells that rely predominantly on aPBPs tend to be wider and shorter.
source: Cells that rely exclusively on the elongasome for growth are longer and thinner, whereas those that rely predominantly on aPBPs tend to be wider and shorter (Dion et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dion et al., 2019.

claim: Many PG synthesis inhibitors activate the σM regulon.
source: Many PG synthesis inhibitors activate the σM regulon, and this leads to elevated expression of many key PG biosynthetic enzymes (MurB, Amj, BcrC), elongasome components (MreB, RodA, MreCD), and the major aPBP (PBP1) (Eiamphungporn and Helmann, 2008; Helmann, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Eiamphungporn and Helmann, 2008; Helmann, 2016.

claim: Activation of the σM regulon leads to elevated expression of many key PG biosynthetic enzymes (MurB, Amj, BcrC), elongasome components (MreB, RodA, MreCD), and the major aPBP (PBP1).
source: Many PG synthesis inhibitors activate the σM regulon, and this leads to elevated expression of many key PG biosynthetic enzymes (MurB, Amj, BcrC), elongasome components (MreB, RodA, MreCD), and the major aPBP (PBP1) (Eiamphungporn and Helmann, 2008; Helmann, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Eiamphungporn and Helmann, 2008; Helmann, 2016.

claim: The ecsAB operon was identified as having numerous mariner transposon insertions in WT, but very few in the Δ4 strain.
source: We identified the ecsAB operon as having numerous mariner transposon insertions in WT, but very few in the Δ4 strain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Tn-Seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: ecsA is essential in the Δ4 background and also with depletion of ponA alone.
source: Interestingly, ecsA was not only essential in the Δ4 background but also with depletion of ponA alone (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by plating efficiency data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: An ΔecsAΔponA mutant was viable when streaked on high Mg plates, and growth was Mg-dependent.
source: Indeed, an ΔecsAΔponA mutant was viable when streaked on high Mg plates, and growth was Mg-dependent (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by growth data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Mutations that impair PG synthesis can often be rescued by growth on plates amended with 20 mM MgSO4.
source: Mutations that impair PG synthesis can often be rescued by growth on plates amended with 20 mM MgSO4, which leads to decreased activity of autolysins and thereby helps restore balance between PG synthesis and degradation pathways (Formstone and Errington, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Formstone and Errington, 2005.

claim: High Mg leads to decreased activity of autolysins and thereby helps restore balance between PG synthesis and degradation pathways.
source: Mutations that impair PG synthesis can often be rescued by growth on plates amended with 20 mM MgSO4, which leads to decreased activity of autolysins and thereby helps restore balance between PG synthesis and degradation pathways (Formstone and Errington, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Formstone and Errington, 2005.

claim: EcsA has been designated as part of an ABC-type transporter involved in the expression and secretion of proteins.
source: EcsA has been designated as part of an ABC-type transporter involved in the expression and secretion of proteins (Leskelä et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Leskelä et al., 1999.

claim: Deletion of ecsA has a profound effect on the intramembrane protease RasP, with similar phenotypes noted for the ecsA and rasP deletion mutants.
source: Deletion of ecsA has a profound effect on the intramembrane protease RasP, with similar phenotypes noted for the ecsA and rasP deletion mutants (Heinrich et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Heinrich et al., 2008.

claim: Viability of ΔrasPΔponA depends on high Mg concentrations.
source: Indeed, viability of ΔrasPΔponA, like ΔecsAΔponA, depended on high Mg concentrations (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by growth data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The EcsAB-RasP pathway is critical in maintaining viability in the absence of aPBPs.
source: The above data highlight the importance of the EcsAB-RasP pathway in maintaining viability in the absence of aPBPs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the synthetic lethality data presented in Figure 1.

claim: ecsA and rasP mutants were moenomycin sensitive with a four-fold decrease in minimum inhibitory concentration relative to WT.
source: Indeed, ecsA and rasP mutants were MOE sensitive with a four-fold decrease in minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) relative to WT (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by MIC data shown in Table 1.

claim: ecsA and rasP single mutants grew as well as WT in the absence of moenomycin, albeit with some lysis in stationary phase.
source: This was not due to a general growth defect: ecsA and rasP single mutants grew as well as WT in the absence of MOE, albeit with some lysis in stationary phase (Figure 2A), consistent with previous observations (Heinrich et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by growth kinetics data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: ΔecsAΔrasP had a similar moenomycin sensitivity as ΔrasP.
source: Moreover, ΔecsAΔrasP had a similar MOE sensitivity as ΔrasP (Figure 2A), suggesting that the synthetic lethality of ecsA with ponA is mediated through its known downstream effect on the activity of RasP (Heinrich et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by growth kinetics data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The synthetic lethality of ecsA with ponA is mediated through its known downstream effect on the activity of RasP.
source: Moreover, ΔecsAΔrasP had a similar MOE sensitivity as ΔrasP (Figure 2A), suggesting that the synthetic lethality of ecsA with ponA is mediated through its known downstream effect on the activity of RasP (Heinrich et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference based on the similar phenotypes and supported by citation to Heinrich et al., 2008.

claim: The ΔrasP and ΔponA mutants had a similar sensitivity as WT when tested for sensitivity to nisin and vancomycin.
source: In contrast to MOE, the ΔrasP and ΔponA mutants had a similar sensitivity as WT when tested for sensitivity to antibiotics that act on substrates common to both the elongasome and aPBP-dependent pathways of PG synthesis. For example, both nisin (Wiedemann et al., 2001) and vancomycin (Watanakunakorn, 1984) bind the common lipid II intermediate (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by disc diffusion assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nisin and vancomycin bind the common lipid II intermediate.
source: For example, both nisin (Wiedemann et al., 2001) and vancomycin (Watanakunakorn, 1984) bind the common lipid II intermediate (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wiedemann et al., 2001 and Watanakunakorn, 1984.

claim: The EcsAB-RasP pathway is critical when aPBPs are compromised, but not as a general response to inhibition of PG synthesis.
source: Together, these results suggest that the EcsAB-RasP pathway is critical when aPBPs are compromised, but not as a general response to inhibition of PG synthesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential sensitivity to different antibiotics.

claim: Oxacillin and cefuroxime preferentially inhibit aPBPs.
source: Oxacillin and cefuroxime (CEF) were previously suggested to preferentially inhibit aPBPs (Sassine et al., 2017; Sharifzadeh et al., 2020), whereas penicillin G preferentially inhibits bPBPs (Sassine et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sassine et al., 2017; Sharifzadeh et al., 2020.

claim: Penicillin G preferentially inhibits bPBPs.
source: Oxacillin and cefuroxime (CEF) were previously suggested to preferentially inhibit aPBPs (Sassine et al., 2017; Sharifzadeh et al., 2020), whereas penicillin G preferentially inhibits bPBPs (Sassine et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sassine et al., 2017.

claim: Oxacillin and cefuroxime had highest activity against ∆rasP.
source: Consistently, oxacillin and CEF had highest activity against ∆rasP, whereas penicillin G and ampicillin had the highest activity against ∆ponA, which encodes the major aPBP, PBP1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by disc diffusion assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Penicillin G and ampicillin had the highest activity against ∆ponA.
source: Consistently, oxacillin and CEF had highest activity against ∆rasP, whereas penicillin G and ampicillin had the highest activity against ∆ponA, which encodes the major aPBP, PBP1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by disc diffusion assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The EcsAB-RasP pathway functionally compensates either for the absence of aPBPs or for their chemical inhibition at either the TG or TP active sites.
source: These results support the idea that the EcsAB-RasP pathway functionally compensates either for the absence of aPBPs or for their chemical inhibition at either the TG (MOE) or TP (CEF) active sites.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the antibiotic sensitivity data.

claim: The ∆ponA mutant was more cefuroxime resistant than WT.
source: Interestingly, the ∆ponA mutant was actually more CEF resistant than WT.
evidence: This is supported by disc diffusion assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Moenomycin and cefuroxime together resulted in synergistic inhibition.
source: In contrast, MOE and CEF together resulted in synergistic inhibition (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by growth kinetics and FIC index data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: RasP proteolytically inactivates the anti-sigma factors RsiW, RsiV and RsgI.
source: RasP proteolytically inactivates the anti-sigma factors RsiW (regulator of σW) (Schöbel et al., 2004), RsiV (regulator of σV) (Hastie et al., 2013) and RsgI (regulator of σI) (Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schöbel et al., 2004; Hastie et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2017.

claim: RasP also cleaves FtsL, a cell division protein.
source: RasP also cleaves FtsL, a cell division protein (Bramkamp et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bramkamp et al., 2006.

claim: The ΔsigI mutant was significantly more sensitive to moenomycin with the MIC being 0.4 µg/mL, similar to ΔrasP.
source: However, the ΔsigI mutant was significantly more sensitive to MOE with the MIC being 0.4 µg/mL, similar to ΔrasP.
evidence: This is supported by MIC data shown in Table 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: σI is required for optimal function of the moenomycin-insensitive elongasome.
source: This suggests that σI is required for optimal function of the MOE-insensitive elongasome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the MOE sensitivity of the ΔsigI mutant.

claim: Of the known RasP targets, σI contributes the most to cefuroxime resistance.
source: Of the known RasP targets, σI contributes the most to CEF resistance.
evidence: This is supported by disc diffusion assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The ΔsigWΔsigI mutant phenocopies the ΔrasP mutant in cefuroxime sensitivity.
source: Moreover, the ΔsigWΔsigI mutant phenocopies the ΔrasP mutant, suggesting that activation of σI and σW largely accounts for the role of RasP in CEF resistance.
evidence: This is supported by disc diffusion assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Activation of σI and σW largely accounts for the role of RasP in cefuroxime resistance.
source: Moreover, the ΔsigWΔsigI mutant phenocopies the ΔrasP mutant, suggesting that activation of σI and σW largely accounts for the role of RasP in CEF resistance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phenocopy observation.

claim: The sensitivity of the ΔecsA and ΔrasP mutants was not further increased by mutation of sigW or sigI.
source: In addition, the sensitivity of the ΔecsA and ΔrasP mutants was not further increased by mutation of sigW or sigI (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), indicative of them being in the same pathway.
evidence: This is supported by disc diffusion assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Deletion of rsgI led to a significant decrease in cefuroxime sensitivity of the ΔecsA and ΔrasP mutants.
source: Finally, deletion of rsgI, encoding the σI anti-sigma factor, led to a significant decrease in CEF sensitivity of the ΔecsA and ΔrasP mutants.
evidence: This is supported by disc diffusion assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: σI plays a dominant role in intrinsic cefuroxime resistance.
source: Thus, σI plays a dominant role in intrinsic CEF resistance, and as expected this activity relies on the RasP-dependent degradation of the RsgI anti-sigma factor.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the genetic epistasis data.

claim: σI activity relies on the RasP-dependent degradation of the RsgI anti-sigma factor.
source: Thus, σI plays a dominant role in intrinsic CEF resistance, and as expected this activity relies on the RasP-dependent degradation of the RsgI anti-sigma factor.
evidence: This is supported by the genetic data and established knowledge about the RasP-RsgI-σI pathway.

claim: The ΔsigIΔponA double mutant could survive with high Mg2+, but was unable to grow on LB.
source: The double mutant could survive with high Mg2+, but was unable to grow on LB.
evidence: This is supported by plating efficiency data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The synthetic lethality of the ΔsigIΔponA and ΔrasPΔponA strains was suppressed by ectopically expressing the sigI gene from the leaky promoter Pspac(hy).
source: This synthetic lethality of the ΔsigIΔponA and ΔrasPΔponA strains was suppressed by ectopically expressing the sigI gene from the leaky promoter Pspac(hy).
evidence: This is supported by plating efficiency data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Decreased σI activity can fully explain the ∆rasP antibiotic sensitivity phenotypes.
source: Thus, decreased σI activity can fully explain the ∆rasP antibiotic sensitivity phenotypes, and we therefore conclude that one or more members of the σI regulon must facilitate growth under conditions of impaired aPBP activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the complementation data.

claim: One or more members of the σI regulon must facilitate growth under conditions of impaired aPBP activity.
source: Thus, decreased σI activity can fully explain the ∆rasP antibiotic sensitivity phenotypes, and we therefore conclude that one or more members of the σI regulon must facilitate growth under conditions of impaired aPBP activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic data.

claim: Five genes directly regulated by σI (mreBH, lytE, gsiB, fabI and bcrC) have known or likely roles related to cell envelope functions.
source: Of the genes directly regulated by σI (Ramaniuk et al., 2018), five (mreBH, lytE, gsiB, fabI and bcrC) have known or likely roles related to cell envelope functions.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about these genes and supported by citation to Ramaniuk et al., 2018.

claim: GsiB is a general stress response protein.
source: GsiB is a general stress response protein (Michna et al., 2016) and FabI is involved in fatty acid synthesis (Heath et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Michna et al., 2016.

claim: FabI is involved in fatty acid synthesis.
source: GsiB is a general stress response protein (Michna et al., 2016) and FabI is involved in fatty acid synthesis (Heath et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Heath et al., 2000.

claim: BcrC functions in undecaprenylpyrophosphate recycling.
source: BcrC functions in undecaprenylpyrophosphate recycling (Bernard et al., 2005; Zhao et al., 2016; Radeck et al., 2017b), and MreBH and LytE are both elongasome-associated proteins.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bernard et al., 2005; Zhao et al., 2016; Radeck et al., 2017b.

claim: MreBH and LytE are both elongasome-associated proteins.
source: BcrC functions in undecaprenylpyrophosphate recycling (Bernard et al., 2005; Zhao et al., 2016; Radeck et al., 2017b), and MreBH and LytE are both elongasome-associated proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by prior literature.

claim: MreBH sequesters and directs the LytE endopeptidase to the sites of insertion of new peptidoglycan.
source: MreBH, one of three MreB-family proteins that associate with the elongasome, sequesters and directs the LytE endopeptidase to the sites of insertion of new peptidoglycan (Carballido-López et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Carballido-López et al., 2006.

claim: The mreBH, lytE and bcrC single mutants exhibited slightly higher sensitivity for both cefuroxime and moenomycin.
source: The mreBH, lytE and bcrC single mutants exhibited slightly higher sensitivity for both CEF and MOE (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), however, they did not entirely phenocopy the sigI phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by disc diffusion and growth kinetics data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ΔmreBHΔlytE double mutant exhibited the same level of cefuroxime and moenomycin sensitivity as both the rasP and sigI mutants.
source: The ΔmreBHΔlytE double mutant exhibited the same level of CEF and MOE sensitivity as both the rasP and sigI mutants (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is supported by disc diffusion and growth kinetics data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: The EcsAB-RasP-σI pathway primarily acts through MreBH and LytE to control elongasome function.
source: Thus, these results suggest that the EcsAB-RasP-σI pathway primarily acts through MreBH and LytE to control elongasome function.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the genetic epistasis data.

claim: A ΔmreBHΔponA double mutant could be constructed only when the cells were initially plated on LB supplemented with high Mg2+.
source: A ΔmreBHΔponA double mutant could be constructed only when the cells were initially plated on LB supplemented with high Mg2+.
evidence: This is supported by plating efficiency data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The ΔmreBHΔponA and ΔlytEΔponA double mutants did not exhibit a plating defect on LB.
source: Once constructed, however, this mutant and the ΔlytEΔponA double mutant did not exhibit a plating defect on LB.
evidence: This is supported by plating efficiency data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The triple mutant of ΔmreBHΔlytEΔponA was synthetic lethal and could not be plated on LB agar without Mg2+ supplementation.
source: In contrast, the triple mutant of ΔmreBHΔlytEΔponA was synthetic lethal and could not be plated on LB agar without Mg2+ supplementation.
evidence: This is supported by plating efficiency data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: MreBH and LytE have an additive role in the effective functioning of the elongasome.
source: These data suggest an additive role for MreBH and LytE in the effective functioning of the elongasome, likely due to the ability of LytE to retain some function in the absence of MreBH, and MreBH having functional roles beyond localization of LytE.
evidence: This is an inference based on the synthetic lethality patterns.

claim: B. subtilis has two partially redundant D,L-endopeptidases, LytE and CwlO, which are collectively essential for cell viability.
source: B. subtilis has two partially redundant D,L-endopeptidases, LytE and CwlO, which are collectively essential for cell viability (Hashimoto et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hashimoto et al., 2012.

claim: Both ΔlytEΔcwlO and ΔsigIΔcwlO are synthetic lethal.
source: The involvement of σI in the expression of lytE has already been established since both ΔlytEΔcwlO and ΔsigIΔcwlO are synthetic lethal (Salzberg et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Salzberg et al., 2013.

claim: ΔrasPΔcwlO was synthetic lethal.
source: Consistently, ΔrasPΔcwlO was also synthetic lethal (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by transformation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ΔlytE mutant had a lower rate of autolysis.
source: By monitoring the time taken for a 50% reduction in optical density, we found that the ΔlytE mutant had a lower rate of autolysis (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by autolysis assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: ΔrasP, ΔsigI and ΔmreBH had lower autolytic potential, consistent with a role in affecting LytE expression or activity.
source: Similar to ΔlytE, we observed that ΔrasP, ΔsigI and ΔmreBH also had lower autolytic potential, consistent with a role in affecting LytE expression or activity.
evidence: This is supported by autolysis assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In the ΔponA mutant, mreBH was significantly upregulated, whereas lytE was unchanged.
source: In the ΔponA mutant, mreBH was significantly upregulated, whereas lytE was unchanged.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: In ΔsigI, both mreBH and lytE expression was significantly lower.
source: In ΔsigI, both mreBH and lytE expression was significantly lower.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: ΔponA cells require higher levels of MreBH to direct the autolytic activity of LytE to support optimal elongasome function.
source: This suggests that ΔponA cells require higher levels of MreBH to direct the autolytic activity of LytE to support optimal elongasome function, and that activation of σI mediates increased mreBH expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the gene expression data.

claim: Activation of σI mediates increased mreBH expression.
source: This suggests that ΔponA cells require higher levels of MreBH to direct the autolytic activity of LytE to support optimal elongasome function, and that activation of σI mediates increased mreBH expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the gene expression data.

claim: Ectopic expression of mreBH complements the cefuroxime sensitivity of ΔmreBH.
source: Although ectopic expression of mreBH complements the CEF sensitivity of ΔmreBH, it is unable to restore CEF resistance to the ΔmreBHΔlytE double mutant (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by disc diffusion assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Ectopic expression of mreBH is unable to restore cefuroxime resistance to the ΔmreBHΔlytE double mutant.
source: Although ectopic expression of mreBH complements the CEF sensitivity of ΔmreBH, it is unable to restore CEF resistance to the ΔmreBHΔlytE double mutant (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by disc diffusion assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: When both mreBH and lytE were ectopically expressed, the strain was significantly more cefuroxime resistant than WT.
source: However, when both mreBH and lytE were ectopically expressed, the strain was significantly more CEF resistant than WT (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by disc diffusion assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Induction of mreBH modestly increased cefuroxime resistance of ΔrasP, but not a ΔrasPΔlytE double mutant.
source: Similarly, induction of mreBH modestly increased CEF resistance of ΔrasP (Figure 5B), but not a ΔrasPΔlytE double mutant.
evidence: This is supported by disc diffusion assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In ΔsigI, mreBH expression alone had no significant impact on cefuroxime resistance.
source: In ΔsigI, however, mreBH expression alone had no significant impact on CEF resistance, perhaps due to reduced availability of LytE.
evidence: This is supported by disc diffusion assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Increasing MreBH levels likely functions to increase elongasome activity by facilitating the localized action of LytE.
source: Thus, increasing MreBH levels likely functions to increase elongasome activity by facilitating the localized action of LytE.
evidence: This is an inference based on the complementation data.

claim: The Pspac(hy)lytE overexpression construct could not be introduced into the ΔrasP and ΔsigI mutants.
source: Conversely, the Pspac(hy)lytE overexpression construct could not be introduced into the ΔrasP and ΔsigI mutants.
evidence: This is an experimental observation indicating synthetic lethality.

claim: High LytE, in cells that have reduced expression of mreBH, leads to delocalized and unregulated autolysin activity.
source: We speculate that high LytE, in cells that have reduced expression of mreBH, leads to delocalized and unregulated autolysin activity.
evidence: This is speculation based on the inability to introduce the lytE overexpression construct.

claim: A major role of MreBH is in directing LytE to sites of ongoing, elongasome-dependent PG synthesis.
source: Collectively, these results further support a model in which a major role of MreBH is in directing LytE to sites of ongoing, elongasome-dependent PG synthesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the complementation and overexpression data.

claim: The elongasome is critical for the maintenance of rod-shape.
source: The elongasome is critical for the maintenance of rod-shape, as judged by the spherical morphology of conditional mutants that are depleted for either the RodA transglycosylase or the two class B PBPs that provide transpeptidase activity (Boylan and Mendelson, 1969; Wei et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Boylan and Mendelson, 1969; Wei et al., 2003.

claim: The maintenance of rod shape is affected by the balance between the directional motion of the elongasome and the random diffusive motion of PBP1.
source: The maintenance of rod shape is also affected by the balance between the directional motion of the elongasome and the random diffusive motion of PBP1 (Dion et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dion et al., 2019.

claim: Overexpression of MreB or other elongasome proteins leads to cells that are longer and thinner.
source: Overexpression of MreB or other elongasome proteins leads to cells that are longer and thinner, whereas overexpression of PBP1 leads to shorter and wider cells (Dion et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dion et al., 2019.

claim: Overexpression of PBP1 leads to shorter and wider cells.
source: Overexpression of MreB or other elongasome proteins leads to cells that are longer and thinner, whereas overexpression of PBP1 leads to shorter and wider cells (Dion et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dion et al., 2019.

claim: ΔrasP, ΔsigI and ΔmreBHΔlytE mutants were significantly shorter and wider compared to the WT.
source: Indeed, ΔrasP, ΔsigI and ΔmreBHΔlytE mutants were significantly shorter (Figure 5C) and wider (Figure 5D) compared to the WT, which indicates that these cells were primarily utilizing PBP1 for PG synthesis.
evidence: This is supported by cell morphology data shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: ΔrasP, ΔsigI and ΔmreBHΔlytE cells were primarily utilizing PBP1 for PG synthesis.
source: Indeed, ΔrasP, ΔsigI and ΔmreBHΔlytE mutants were significantly shorter (Figure 5C) and wider (Figure 5D) compared to the WT, which indicates that these cells were primarily utilizing PBP1 for PG synthesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cell morphology data.

claim: ΔmreBH and ΔlytE mutants individually had lower elongasome activity.
source: ΔmreBH and ΔlytE mutants individually also had lower elongasome activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the cell morphology data shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: The ΔponA mutant formed significantly thinner cells due to PG synthesis being contributed mainly by the elongasome.
source: In contrast, the ΔponA mutant formed significantly thinner cells due to PG synthesis being contributed mainly by the elongasome.
evidence: This is supported by cell morphology data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The rasP, sigI and mreBH-lytE genes all support elongasome function.
source: These data support the conclusion that the rasP, sigI and mreBH-lytE genes all support elongasome function.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the cell morphology data.

claim: Three suppressor strains with point mutations in walK (Ala241Asp, Ser385Leu, Asp274Ala) were identified.
source: Using whole-genome resequencing, we identified three strains with point mutations in walK (Ala241Asp, Ser385Leu, Asp274Ala).
evidence: This is supported by whole-genome sequencing data.

claim: WalK is the sensor kinase of the essential two-component system WalKR, which regulates cell wall metabolism.
source: WalK is the sensor kinase of the essential two-component system WalKR, which regulates cell wall metabolism (Takada and Yoshikawa, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Takada and Yoshikawa, 2018.

claim: WalR has binding sites upstream of sigI, mreBH and lytE and activates expression of these genes under heat stress.
source: WalR has binding sites upstream of sigI, mreBH and lytE and activates expression of these genes under heat stress (Huang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Huang et al., 2013.

claim: WalR may function in conjunction with the σA holoenzyme, which together with σI controls lytE expression.
source: WalR may function in conjunction with the σA holoenzyme, which together with σI controls lytE expression (Tseng et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tseng et al., 2011.

claim: Residue 274 of WalK lies in the cytoplasmic Per-Arnt-Sim (PAS) domain.
source: Residue 274 lies in the cytoplasmic Per-Arnt-Sim (PAS) domain of WalK (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by the domain structure shown in Figure 6A.

claim: PAS domains have been linked to signal sensing.
source: PAS domains have been linked to signal sensing (Taylor and Zhulin, 1999) and may be involved in protein dimerization (Huang et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Taylor and Zhulin, 1999; Huang et al., 1993.

claim: The cytoplasmic PAS domain of S. aureus WalK was found to bind zinc at a site including D274.
source: Recently, the cytoplasmic PAS domain of S. aureus WalK was found to bind zinc at a site including D274.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Monk et al., 2019 as referenced in the manuscript.

claim: Mutation in the zinc binding site of S. aureus WalK led to increased kinase activity.
source: Moreover, mutation in this binding site, which is highly conserved in WalK orthologs (Monk et al., 2019), led to increased kinase activity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Monk et al., 2019.

claim: The WalKD274A suppressor led to increased activity of the WalKR two-component system.
source: We therefore hypothesized that the WalKD274A suppressor (denoted as WalK*) led to increased activity of the WalKR two-component system.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the known function of the D274 residue.

claim: The walK* allele suppressed the synthetic lethality of ΔrasPΔponA.
source: We used CRISPR mutagenesis to introduce the walK* allele into WT cells and then confirmed that this allele suppressed the synthetic lethality of ΔrasPΔponA (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by spot dilution assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: walK* increased cefuroxime resistance of the ΔrasP strain, but could not rescue the ΔsigI strain.
source: Although walK* increased CEF resistance of the ΔrasP strain, it could not rescue the ΔsigI strain.
evidence: This is supported by disc diffusion assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: WalR may act in conjunction with σI to activate transcription of mreBH.
source: This supports the idea that WalR may act in conjunction with σI to activate transcription of mreBH, and thereby augment elongasome activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic epistasis data.

claim: Increased activation of WalK* can lead to increased expression of not only lytE, but also cwlO.
source: Increased activation of WalK* can lead to increased expression of not only lytE, but also cwlO (Takada and Yoshikawa, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Takada and Yoshikawa, 2018.

claim: The walK* allele led to increased expression of both mreBH and lytE.
source: The walK* allele led to increased expression of both mreBH and lytE.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The mreBH and lytE expression levels in walK* were similar to that observed in the ΔponA background.
source: Moreover, these levels were similar to that observed in the ΔponA background, suggesting that deletion of ponA leads to a compensatory increase in mreBH and lytE mediated by the WalKR.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Deletion of ponA leads to a compensatory increase in mreBH and lytE mediated by the WalKR.
source: Moreover, these levels were similar to that observed in the ΔponA background, suggesting that deletion of ponA leads to a compensatory increase in mreBH and lytE mediated by the WalKR.
evidence: This is an inference based on the gene expression data.

claim: walK* leads to increased activation of WalR, which then leads to increased transcription of sigI and thereby of mreBH and lytE.
source: These data suggest that walK* leads to increased activation of WalR, which then leads to increased transcription of sigI and thereby of mreBH and lytE.
evidence: This is an inference based on the gene expression and genetic epistasis data.

claim: The extracytoplasmic (ECF) sigma factor σM plays a significant role in B. subtilis cell wall homeostasis.
source: While our results suggest a critical role for σI in aPBP-elongasome homeostasis through its regulation of MreBH and LytE, previous studies have indicated that the extracytoplasmic (ECF) sigma factor σM also plays a significant role in B. subtilis cell wall homeostasis.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by prior literature.

claim: σM regulates the expression of rodA, mreB, mreC and mreD, as well as ponA and other genes involved in PG synthesis.
source: σM regulates the expression of rodA, mreB, mreC and mreD (core components of the elongasome), as well as ponA and other genes involved in PG synthesis (Eiamphungporn and Helmann, 2008; Luo and Helmann, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Eiamphungporn and Helmann, 2008; Luo and Helmann, 2012.

claim: The cefuroxime sensitivity of PM*rodA and PM*rodA-PM*maf was similar to that of the sigM mutant.
source: The CEF sensitivity of PM*rodA and PM*rodA-PM*maf was similar to that of the sigM mutant (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by disc diffusion assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Under conditions where cefuroxime has inhibited PBP1, σM helps restore peptidoglycan synthesis primarily by increasing the expression of rodA to increase elongasome activity.
source: Thus, under conditions where CEF has inhibited PBP1, σM helps restore peptidoglycan synthesis primarily by increasing the expression of rodA to increase elongasome activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the promoter mutant data.

claim: The double mutants of ΔecsAΔsigM, ΔrasPΔsigM and ΔsigIΔsigM revealed an additive effect with respect to cefuroxime sensitivity.
source: In contrast, the double mutants of ΔecsAΔsigM, ΔrasPΔsigM and ΔsigIΔsigM revealed an additive effect with respect to CEF sensitivity (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by disc diffusion assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The role of the elongasome in PG synthesis can be regulated through two independent pathways: the EcsAB-RasP-σI pathway acts by regulating MreBH and LytE, and the σM pathway acts through RodA.
source: Thus, the role of the elongasome in PG synthesis can be regulated through two-independent pathways: the EcsAB-RasP-σI pathway acts by regulating MreBH and LytE, and the σM pathway acts through RodA.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the genetic epistasis data.

claim: During growth, PG is continuously remodeled, which involves the action of autolysins, hydrolytic enzymes that cleave links within and between the glycan strands.
source: During growth, PG is continuously remodeled, which involves the action of autolysins, hydrolytic enzymes that cleave links within and between the glycan strands (Vollmer et al., 2008; Egan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Vollmer et al., 2008; Egan et al., 2020.

claim: Hydrolases are essential for the insertion of new glycan strands into the existing structure.
source: These hydrolases are essential for the insertion of new glycan strands into the existing structure (Hashimoto et al., 2012; Singh et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hashimoto et al., 2012; Singh et al., 2012.

claim: Cell shape maintenance requires that the sites of new PG synthesis be spatially regulated, often in response to the activity of cytoskeletal filaments such as MreB and FtsZ proteins.
source: Cell shape maintenance requires that the sites of new PG synthesis be spatially regulated, often in response to the activity of cytoskeletal filaments such as the MreB (Domínguez-Escobar et al., 2011) and FtsZ proteins (Mahone and Goley, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Domínguez-Escobar et al., 2011; Mahone and Goley, 2020.

claim: There are three MreB paralogs in B. subtilis (MreB, Mbl and MreBH), which colocalize to form elongasome-associated cytoskeletal filaments along the cell periphery.
source: In B. subtilis, there are three MreB paralogs (MreB, Mbl and MreBH), which colocalize to form elongasome-associated cytoskeletal filaments along the cell periphery (Carballido-López et al., 2006; Garner et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Carballido-López et al., 2006; Garner et al., 2011.

claim: Cells lacking all three MreB paralogs lose their rod shape and become spheres which ultimately lyse.
source: Cells lacking all three paralogs lose their rod shape and become spheres which ultimately lyse (Kawai et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kawai et al., 2009.

claim: MreB and Mbl are critical for the circumferential motion of the elongasome.
source: Whereas MreB and Mbl are critical for the circumferential motion of the elongasome, the role of MreBH is less clear, and seems related to its ability to recruit LytE (Carballido-López et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Carballido-López et al., 2006.

claim: The role of MreBH is less clear, and seems related to its ability to recruit LytE.
source: Whereas MreB and Mbl are critical for the circumferential motion of the elongasome, the role of MreBH is less clear, and seems related to its ability to recruit LytE (Carballido-López et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Carballido-López et al., 2006.

claim: PG synthesis by the elongasome relies on the activity of RodA as transglycosylase, with bPBPs providing transpeptidase activity.
source: PG synthesis by the elongasome relies on the activity of RodA as TG, with bPBPs providing TP activity (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is established knowledge illustrated in Figure 8A.

claim: The σM response is selectively induced by stresses during PG synthesis and contributes to resistance to a wide-variety of PG synthesis inhibitors, including moenomycin, cefuroxime, and bacitracin.
source: The σM response is selectively induced by stresses during PG synthesis and contributes to resistance to a wide-variety of PG synthesis inhibitors, including MOE, CEF, and bacitracin (Helmann, 2016; Mascher et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Helmann, 2016; Mascher et al., 2007.

claim: The σM regulon serves to both upregulate PG synthetic capacity, and to compensate for stresses resulting from PG inhibition.
source: The σM regulon serves to both upregulate PG synthetic capacity, and to compensate for stresses resulting from PG inhibition.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the σM regulon.

claim: The σM regulon includes the up-regulation of elongasome components and PG biosynthetic enzymes (PBP1, Ddl, MurB, MurF, BcrC, Amj).
source: The former includes the up-regulation of elongasome components (Figure 8A) and PG biosynthetic enzymes (PBP1, Ddl, MurB, MurF, BcrC, Amj) (Eiamphungporn and Helmann, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Eiamphungporn and Helmann, 2008.

claim: The σM regulon includes the large regulon controlled by the Spx transcription factor that protects cells against antibiotic-associated oxidative stress.
source: The latter includes the large regulon controlled by the Spx transcription factor that protects cells against antibiotic-associated oxidative stress (Rojas-Tapias and Helmann, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rojas-Tapias and Helmann, 2018.

claim: Induction of a σM-regulated ppGpp synthase, YwaC, increases the number of persister cells following antibiotic exposure.
source: Finally, it has recently been shown that induction of a σM-regulated ppGpp synthase, YwaC, increases the number of persister cells following antibiotic exposure (Fung et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fung et al., 2020.

claim: Induction of σI selectively elevates elongasome function by increasing the expression of the MreB paralog, MreBH, and the associated autolytic endopeptidase LytE.
source: Here, we identify a major role for another alternative sigma factor, σI, in conferring intrinsic resistance to important cell wall antibiotics, MOE and CEF. Induction of σI, which requires the EcsAB-RasP regulatory pathway (Liu et al., 2017), selectively elevates elongasome function by increasing the expression of the MreB paralog, MreBH, and the associated autolytic endopeptidase LytE (Carballido-López et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: This stress response is critical in cells lacking PBP1.
source: This stress response is critical in cells lacking PBP1, as judged by the synthetic lethality of ΔsigI ΔponA mutants (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by synthetic lethality data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: This stress response functions in coordination with both the σM stress response and the essential WalKR two-component system.
source: This stress response functions in coordination with both the σM stress response (Figure 7A), which increases elongasome function by upregulation of the RodA TG (Meeske et al., 2016; Emami et al., 2017), and the essential WalKR two-component system (Figures 6 and 8).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the genetic epistasis data shown in Figures 6, 7, and 8.

claim: σI was previously linked to heat-stress, virulence in B. anthracis, and control of autolysin synthesis.
source: Although σI was previously linked to heat-stress (Zuber et al., 2001), virulence in B. anthracis (Kim and Wilson, 2016), and control of autolysin synthesis (Salzberg et al., 2013), our results reveal new insights into its role in cell envelope stress.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zuber et al., 2001; Kim and Wilson, 2016; Salzberg et al., 2013.

claim: WalR, σI and σA binding sites have been previously annotated in the promoters of sigI, mreBH and lytE.
source: WalR, σI and σA binding sites have been previously annotated in the promoters of sigI, mreBH and lytE (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is established knowledge illustrated in Figure 8B.

claim: The WalK (D274A) gain of function mutant suppresses the lethal phenotype of ΔrasPΔponA by induction of mreBH and lytE.
source: The WalK (D274A) gain of function mutant suppresses the lethal phenotype of ΔrasPΔponA by induction of mreBH and lytE (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by suppressor analysis and gene expression data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Co-activation by WalR and σI is required for induction of mreBH and lytE.
source: We conclude that co-activation by WalR and σI is required for induction of these two genes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the genetic epistasis data.

claim: The signals sensed by WalK are unclear.
source: The signals sensed by WalK are unclear, but it was recently suggested that peptidoglycan cleavage products generated by LytE and CwlO can be sensed by WalK to balance the activity of these proteins (Dobihal et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dobihal et al., 2019.

claim: Peptidoglycan cleavage products generated by LytE and CwlO can be sensed by WalK to balance the activity of these proteins.
source: The signals sensed by WalK are unclear, but it was recently suggested that peptidoglycan cleavage products generated by LytE and CwlO can be sensed by WalK to balance the activity of these proteins (Dobihal et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dobihal et al., 2019.

claim: sigI activation enhances the growth of mbl mutants.
source: Moreover, it was previously observed that sigI activation enhances the growth of mbl mutants (Schirner and Errington, 2009), which we suggest was likely due to increasing elongasome activity through mreBH and lytE.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schirner and Errington, 2009.

claim: WalKR and σI act in coordination to maintain optimal elongasome activity.
source: Collectively, our results reveal that WalKR and σI act in coordination to maintain optimal elongasome activity, and these pathways complement the general PG stress response activated by σM (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the collective experimental data illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: PG synthesis involves multiple, functionally overlapping systems, often with one being inducible by antibiotic inhibition of the other.
source: One general theme that has emerged is that PG synthesis involves multiple, functionally overlapping systems, often with one being inducible by antibiotic inhibition of the other.
evidence: This is a general conclusion based on the findings of this study and prior literature.

claim: The inducible UPP phosphatase BcrC complements the activity of UppP.
source: For example, the inducible UPP phosphatase BcrC complements the activity of UppP (Radeck et al., 2017b; Zhao et al., 2016), and the σM-regulated Amj functions as a second lipid II flippase that is critical when MurJ is inhibited (Chamakura et al., 2017; Meeske et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Radeck et al., 2017b; Zhao et al., 2016.

claim: The σM-regulated Amj functions as a second lipid II flippase that is critical when MurJ is inhibited.
source: For example, the inducible UPP phosphatase BcrC complements the activity of UppP (Radeck et al., 2017b; Zhao et al., 2016), and the σM-regulated Amj functions as a second lipid II flippase that is critical when MurJ is inhibited (Chamakura et al., 2017; Meeske et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chamakura et al., 2017; Meeske et al., 2015.

claim: Inhibition of aPBPs by moenomycin leads to an essential, compensatory induction of RodA.
source: Similarly, inhibition of aPBPs by MOE leads to an essential, compensatory induction of RodA (Meeske et al., 2016; Emami et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Meeske et al., 2016; Emami et al., 2017.

claim: This single σM-regulated target gene (rodA) can largely account for the cefuroxime sensitivity of sigM mutants.
source: Here, it is shown that this single σM-regulated target gene can largely account for the CEF sensitivity of sigM mutants (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by promoter mutant data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The increase in RodA, together with the induction of MreBH and LytE, serves to boost the biosynthetic potential of the elongasome.
source: This increase in RodA, together with the induction of MreBH and LytE, serves to boost the biosynthetic potential of the elongasome.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the collective experimental data.

claim: These results reveal mechanisms that allow diverse PG biosynthetic complexes to coordinate their activities, in both time and space.
source: These results reveal mechanisms that allow diverse PG biosynthetic complexes to coordinate their activities, in both time and space.
evidence: This is a general conclusion based on the findings of the study.

claim: The highly orchestrated processes that direct and coordinate PG synthesis are important both for intrinsic antibiotic resistance and are ultimately responsible for the enormous diversity of bacterial morphologies.
source: The highly orchestrated processes that direct and coordinate PG synthesis are important both for intrinsic antibiotic resistance, as explored here and are ultimately responsible for the enormous diversity of bacterial morphologies (Caccamo and Brun, 2018).
evidence: This is a general conclusion supported by citation to Caccamo and Brun, 2018.
